newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - N.Electric says not last defence.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - N.Electric says not last defence.

text.p: British regional electricity company Northern Electric will give more information on its value, after half year results and year forecasts to fend off CE Electric's hostile bid, chairman David Morris said.
"This is not our last defence document...we will be pointing out prospects, highlighting areas of value," he told Reuters in a telephone interview.
Northern brought out half year results just under a week early on Friday and made forecasts for the year as part of its defence against the 630 pence per share offer.
Northern said interim pretax profits slipped to 50.7 million stg from 58.7 million stg and paid out a dividend of 12.85 pence, up from 12.0 pence.
Year profits would be over 112 million stg with a final dividend of 29.85 pence and gearing would fall to 95 percent.
"We are simply pointing out the value of Northern Electric," Morris said, adding that if the UK government approved the bid, the figures would be more fully appreciated.
"You will see a vast change then," he said.
Northern's shares are currently languishing at around 600 pence, weighed by concerns the government might block the bid.
Morris said the shareholders would ultimately decide the value of the company, but stressed the figures showed "we have absolutely got our finger on the pulse."
Northern argued in its statement that based on 1997 forecast cash flow, it should be valued at 745 pence.
"We would talk around 700 pence...(but) it is quite clear we were looking for more than 700 pence," Morris said.
Northern has said it felt the bid should be approved by government but has maintained that 630 pence did not represent its true value.

Morris said the group's improved cash flow benefited from several factors including some proceeds and profit from the sale of First Hydro, the pumped storage business of National Grid, which had been held back.
Northern said a year ago it would retain 44 million stg which it received from it 6.47 percent stake in First Hydro.
Morris added that refinancing of the company's Teeside power station at improved interest rates had also helped.

He said the government's proposed changes to capital allowances for long-term assets, put forward in Tuesday's budget, would have a "very minimal" effect on Northern, with around three million stg in extra tax annually seen "well beyond 2000."
